sources.title: RIT CSCI-351 Data Communications and Networks catalog description
sources.author: Rochester Institute of Technology
sources.content: This course is an in-depth study of data communications and networks. The course covers design of, and algorithms and protocols used in, the physical, data link, network, transport, and application layers in the Internet; methods for modeling and analyzing networks, including graphs, graph algorithms, and discrete event simulation; and an introduction to network science. Programming projects will be required. Pre-requisites: CSCI-251 and (MATH-251 or STAT-251 or STAT-205) or equivalent courses. Students cannot take and receive credit for this course if they have taken CSCI-651. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall

sources.title: RFC 1122 Requirements for Internet Hosts
sources.author: Internet Engineering Task Force
sources.content: Internet hosts implement layered link, internet, transport, and application functions. The link layer moves frames across a directly connected network. IP provides best-effort datagram delivery across interconnected networks. An IP address identifies an interface for internet-layer delivery. Routing selects a next hop toward a destination. Transport protocols add endpoint communication functions above IP. Application protocols define the meaning of exchanged data. Correct analysis distinguishes addresses, routes, packets, frames, sockets, and end-to-end state.

sources.title: RFC 9293 Transmission Control Protocol
sources.author: Internet Engineering Task Force
sources.content: TCP provides a reliable, ordered byte stream between endpoints. Sequence numbers identify positions in that byte stream. Acknowledgments report which data has been received. Retransmission recovers data that is presumed lost. Flow control prevents a sender from exceeding the receiver's advertised capacity. A TCP connection moves through defined protocol states. Connection establishment synchronizes endpoint state before application data transfer. Packet loss, duplication, reordering, delay, and endpoint failure must be separated when reasoning about behavior and performance.
